name: The Epistolary Genre: Reading Letters in Context

objectives.text: Identify that some books of the Bible are letters written to churches and to people
Name Paul, Peter, James, and John as people who wrote letters found in the New Testament
Recall that New Testament letters were sent both to whole churches and to individual people
Identify the sender, the recipients, and the greeting in the opening verses of a New Testament letter
Describe the usual parts of a New Testament letter, including the opening, thanksgiving, body, and closing
Explain from the letters themselves that the apostles wrote to teach, correct, and encourage churches
Distinguish the letters of Paul from the General Epistles by their authors and recipients
Compare a personal letter such as Philemon with a letter written to a church such as Ephesians
Locate the cities and regions that received New Testament letters on a map of the Roman world
Identify co-senders named in letter openings, such as Timothy and Silvanus, and explain their connection to the author
Outline the flow of thought of a short New Testament letter section by section
Analyze the occasional nature of the epistles by using clues in the text to reconstruct the situation a letter addresses
Explain how New Testament letters were carried, read aloud to congregations, and shared among churches
Compose a letter that follows the structure of a New Testament epistle to explain the teaching of a chosen passage
Connect the doctrinal teaching of a letter to the commands that follow from it, distinguishing indicative from imperative
Interpret the cultural background of a specific command and distinguish the abiding principle from its first-century expression
Explain the role of the amanuensis in the writing of New Testament letters using evidence from the text
Trace the argument of an epistle by analyzing connecting words such as therefore, for, and but
Construct a historical and cultural background profile of a recipient city such as Corinth and explain how it illuminates the letter
Analyze how the stated theme of a letter governs the development of its argument
Evaluate principles for applying letters written to first-century churches to the church today, including the Reformed principle that Scripture interprets Scripture
Defend the authority of the apostolic letters as Scripture using the testimony of the New Testament and the Reformed confessions
Synthesize Paul's teaching on justification by faith across several of his epistles
Compare the teaching of Paul and James on faith and works and explain how the Reformed tradition harmonizes them

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies (identifying letters, letter parts, occasional nature, indicative and imperative, cultural background, amanuensis, Corinth profile, application today, apostolic authority, Pauline synthesis). Merged greeting observation into identifying sender, recipients, and greeting. Added missing competencies: General Epistles vs Pauline letters, mapping recipients, outlining a letter, delivery and public reading, composing a letter in epistolary form, tracing argument through connectives, theme governing argument, and Paul and James on faith and works. Narrowed the final synthesis to a specific doctrine and added verse-level Scripture and confession anchors throughout.
